title: An Earth-sized procedural planet in Unity 6: from 4,600 km down to grass level, prototyping game graphics tech
author: imlo2
selftext:
One planet with Earth's radius, all procedural, rendered live in Unity 6 (URP).   
The planet is currently rendered in approx. 1.5m geometric accuracy, and finer details are rendered with textures and compute-shader-based systems are used for undergrowth and tree instancing.

The procedural system can place roughly a trillion trees and about as many rocks across the planet deterministically, and the goal is to have walkable near-field resolution and details.

Excluding the short intro to different biomes and environments, the flight is one continuous take captured from the orbit to grassroots level: from a crescent at 4,600km, through the clouds to forest at 70m, a skim over a meadow, up to the edge of space, and then a bit more of flying around to show how it renders and LODs.

**Why:** This is a sister project of my wilderness procedural generator, which focuces on 15-25km2 islands (currently it's a much more detailed environment system), and borrows variety of parts from there.

I'm currently exploring if this could have some use for a game I'd want to make, similar to the wilderness project.

**Terrain:** a cube-sphere quadtree where every tile is the same 32×32 grid, generated on the GPU on the fly. Height is 25 octaves of 3D gradient noise, from 16,000km down to about 1m. The finest tiles are about 49 m across, 1.5m between vertices. Land forms, lakes and mountains are procedurally shaped with different types of processes.

**Precision:** The camera never leaves the origin, and its position is kept in doubles. Because of that, URP's TAA never sees the camera travel, so to get around this the travel is fed into its previous view-projection.

**Sky:** Hillaire's 2020 atmosphere, marched per pixel. Ozone sampled at three wavelengths, as in the reference, and it's averaged over broad RGB bands.

**Climate:** Winds carry rain inland from the seas and drop it over mountains. That decides where clouds, snow, forests and grass go. The planet is mostly desert by choice.

**Clouds:** Volumetric, from a global weather map, traced at half resolution and accumulated over frames.

**Sea:** The terrain clamped to sea level (no underwater areas yet), so there's no second surface to z-fight with. Shaded after Bruneton, Neyret and Holzschuch 2010.

**Trees and grass:** trees grown in my other project's "tree lab", which follows the concepts presented by Palubicki et al. 2009, and impostors from about 100m and shaded canopy beyond 2.5km. Approx. 100,000 GPU grass blades a frame reach 250m, vaguely similar-ish to how it's done Ghost of Tsushima.

**Ground:** Nothing hand-painted, it's all procedural.

**Performance** Currently it runs at about 9-13ms at 1080p in the Editor on an RTX 3090.

**How and why Claude/AI was used:** I've worked for decades with 3D graphics, environment art, shaders and tech art, with some graphics programming. Years ago I wrote a simple cube-sphere planet system, and have created parts and bits needed for this kind of systems (like atmosphere rendering, clouds, etc.) but earlier I deemed this kind of things too monumental to do solo. Last summer I picked the idea up again with coding agents, first Codex earlier and then Claude Code. They write most of the code, I set the direction and the look, choose the references and techniques at times, and judge every change by eye. Texture generation, seam processing, derived maps etc. are all automatically created by agents, they use image generation models and tools built to process the images. Some parts, like the grass and the tree lab, came from my previous project, Wilderness. Music made with Suno.

replies.author: pehmeateemu
replies.body:
I would argue it's the first steps into massive procedurally generated and rich worlds. These tech demos, when observed up close, are empty. There is nothing in this world but to walk around an empty planet filled with trees and water. 

Game content needs a lot of things to do within reasonable space or it becomes a travel simulator. Massive worlds need a huge amount of *variance* in things to do or the experience is more of the same with different skins which means everything built needs testing which means you need a) a lot of spare time b) a big team of playtesters, preferably both and more than a solo dev working with an army of AI agents. Even a thousand agents working on a world of Earth scale will take years to create enough tested PG content to make it feel alive. 

Let's do a little thought experiment - Let's assume we are generating the real world procedurally. For simplicitys sake let's assume only a 100 million people in the world impact how the world looks and feels. Assuming a single agent can do the impact of a 100 people at 100 times faster it would mean 10000 agents are required to make the world a living place. This assumes no timeframe since that is next to impossible to determine. We need a human in the loop to test and analyse if it feels right which leads to my third point.

AI agents are quite terrible at assessing actual gameplay and feel. And will remain so for quite some time. Meanwhile humans will need to feel out every feature and that can not be rushed or the game will feel rushed.

That's the AI that makes enemy NPC's negotiate terrain, CPU chess moves in a game and the most consistently widely used AI that paved the way for all this big data AI: the Google search. People have totally lost the concepts of what AI even means anymore...it's like a damn buzz word now.

comments.body:
anybody working on unity work massive projects know exactly what this is, if you make a game few KMs big the camera and physics begin to act funky due to Floating-Point Precision Error.  in order to fix this in unity, you need to move the world around the player so the player never really leaves the point of origin. 

pretty cool stuff, but anybody could do this.  impostors, world streaming, dots, ecr, GPU instancing, group LOD, did I miss anything ;)

the fun part comes when you actually make a game from it, and find all the performance issues putting together a massive game, and fixing it bit by bit. 

I actually have the biggest mmorpg in the world right now and it fucking works, synced wheather, wind, calendar (day/night cycle), everything authorative by the server :)
maybe one day I will post my mmorpg here when I feel like it has a decent playable loop.

comments.author: LittleYo
comments.body:
Awesome work! Could you share some tips on procedural terrain generation algorithms?

What I've got so far is basically endless, procedurally generated terrain in Godot, but my algorithms suck, and the result looks kinda dull.

My idea was to use one algorithm to generate an endless desert, then layer some additional algorithms on top to create mountain ranges here and there.

I'm particularly interested in how you generate large-scale landforms, especially mountain ranges. Are they created using separate algorithms layered on top of the base noise, with some kind of spatial masks controlling their placement? Or is there a more sophisticated geological simulation involved?

I'm trying to avoid the typical "noise everywhere" look and get more believable, geographically coherent landscapes.
